title: KV index skew during host hot-swap — triage notes and preliminary runbook
content:
TL;DR:
During a routine host hot-swap event on 2024-10-26 we observed progressive divergence of the KV index across a subset of runtime pods (kv_index_skew_ratio > 0.25). Divergence correlated with a short window of elevated host swap churn and a subsequent microbatching backlog that pushed memory usage on affected pods to >95% of allocatable. Several pods hit eviction thresholds and experienced transient request stalls; two pods entered an OOM kill path. This doc captures the on-call timeline, immediate mitigations, debugging commands, reproducibility notes, and a draft runbook to reduce blast radius on future host swaps.

Symptom summary:
- Alerts fired: kv-index-skew-warning (P2), microbatch-queue-length spike (P2), host-memory-pressure (P1 for two hosts).
- User-facing: short-lived increase in token-latency p95 for the hosted API (~300ms extra for ~3 min). No major error-rate increase (5xx stayed within SLO).
- Metric of interest: kv_index_skew_ratio (ratio of divergent KV entries per pod) increased from ~0.01 baseline to 0.32 on affected pods.
- Impact: 2 pods OOM-killed and restarted; these were later found to be in the middle of rebuilds and had large resident sets.

Timeline (as recorded during on-call):
- 2024-10-26 06:12 UTC: Scheduled host hot-swap (rolling upgrade) started for pool-gpu-02.
- 06:16 UTC: microbatch-queue-length metric begins to climb and a few requests see queueing beyond 200ms.
- 06:18 UTC: kv-index-skew-warning alerts fire for pods runtime-02, runtime-07, runtime-11.
- 06:20 UTC: affected pods show concurrent rebuild activity (kv_rebuild_rate spikes) while host-swap still in progress.
- 06:24 UTC: host memory pressure alert for host-12; two pods on host-12 show RSS > 95% of allocatable.
- 06:27 UTC: pod runtime-11 OOM-killed, restarted by k8s; post-restart it rejoined with a fresh index but some client requests experienced 5xx during restart window.
- 06:35 UTC: hot-swap finished, some host-level swapback operations triggered; kv_index_skew_ratio returns toward baseline after rebuilds complete by 06:48 UTC.

Quick investigative notes and commands used:
- Identify divergent pods: runbook-dashboard -> KV Cache -> "KV index skew by pod". Graph query used: sum(divergent_kv_entries) / sum(kv_entries) by (pod).
- Inspect pod logs (grep for rebuild/reconcile):
  kubectl -n runtime logs runtime-11 -c runtime --since=30m | egrep "rebuild|reconcile|index.*skew|kv-evict"
- Check host dmesg / kubelet logs for OOM reasons: ssh node host-12; journalctl -u kubelet -b --no-pager | egrep "oom|evict|killed process"
- Snapshot heap + allocation histograms: curl http://localhost:9090/debug/pprof/heap > /tmp/runtime-heap-$(date +%s).prof (requires local port-forward if remote)
- Correlate microbatch backlog: query microbatch_queue_length{pod=~"runtime-.*"} and microbatch_processing_latency_ms. Noted backlog coinciding with rebuild windows.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Host hot-swap triggers a brief disruption in network connectivity to shared KV metadata store (or ephemeral lock lease anomaly) which causes concurrent rebuild attempts and partial index divergence when multiple pods try to reconstruct missing entries. Rebuilds increase memory usage briefly and when combined with microbatch backlog pushes pods into memory pressure.
2) A race between the rebuild coordinator and ongoing request-driven prefix caching: rebuild writes partial index entries while request code expects a consistent index snapshot. This produces inconsistent indexes that get detected as skew.
3) A regeneration bug where the KV rebuild path temporarily holds large temporary buffers (copy-on-write) when host-side storage is remote-mount backed (seen on host-12), leading to RSS surges.

Immediate mitigations executed during on-call:
- Rate-limited incoming traffic to affected route for 8 minutes (via runtime-route-throttle) to reduce microbatch generation and give rebuilds time to complete. This reduced microbatch_queue_length by ~60% in 3 minutes.
- Temporarily disabled aggressive rebuild concurrency (dynconfig: kv.rebuild.max_concurrency -> 1) via safety rollforward to slow memory growth while retaining availability.
- Eviction tuning: increased eviction headroom for pool-gpu-02 hosts (+10% reserve) to avoid immediate OOM for warm rebuilds. This was rolled back once stable.

How to reproduce (dev env):
- Test plan: simulate a host swap by bringing down a node with many runtime pods while simultaneously generating steady microbatch load with many short requests (seq length ~128).
- Local repro steps:
  1) Deploy two runtime pods with shared kv metadata pointed to local redis mock.
  2) Start a generator that sends requests at ~150rps to both pods.
  3) Kill one pod's host (kubectl drain <node>) or restart kubelet to simulate swap; watch for rebuild/reconcile logs.
  4) Observe memory profiles and kv_index_skew_ratio metric.
- Note: the exact timing window matters — need concurrency between rebuild initiation and request-driven prefix caching to reproduce skew reliably.

Preliminary runbook (draft) — for on-call use during a host hot-swap incident with KV index skew:
- Trigger criteria: kv_index_skew_ratio > 0.2 for > 2 minutes OR kv_rebuild_rate > 5/min AND microbatch_queue_length p95 > 200ms
- Immediate steps:
  1) Identify affected pods via dashboard; mark them as "rebuild-in-progress" in incident doc.
  2) Apply traffic shaping to affected routes (runtime-route-throttle) at -50% to reduce new request load.
  3) Set dynconfig kv.rebuild.max_concurrency=1 for the cluster to serialize rebuilds (safe rollback plan in place).
  4) If host-level memory pressure present, increase host eviction headroom for the pool being swapped (temporary).
  5) If pods are in a rebuild loop and memory rising, cordon host and gradually migrate non-critical pods to other healthy hosts to spread rebuilds.
  6) After rebuilds complete and kv_index_skew_ratio < 0.05 for 5 minutes, progressively revert throttles and restore dynconfig.
- Diagnostic commands to run during runbook execution (copy into on-call checklist):
  - kubectl get pods -l app=runtime -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Running
  - kubectl logs <pod> -c runtime --since=15m | egrep "rebuild|reconcile|kv-"
  - prometheus query: increase(kv_rebuild_count[5m]) by (pod)
  - top/htop on host; docker stats for container rss; journalctl -u kubelet | egrep "evict|oom"

Follow-ups and engineering work items (owner suggestions):
- Short term (SRE + serving-runtime): add a rebuild-phase metric (rebuild_phase{pod,phase}) so we can correlate exact phases with memory deltas. Owner: Marcus Li (SRE) - due 2024-11-15.
- Mid term (infra/serving-runtime): implement cooperative backoff when multiple pods detect missing KV regions so rebuilds are staggered instead of concurrent. Owner: Sofia Alvarez - PR draft 3124 linked.
- Long term (platform): validate host hot-swap sequence to ensure lease propagation to the shared KV metadata store is robust; consider holding off host decommission until rebuilds drain below threshold. Owner: Tom Becker - RFC Q1 2025.

Open questions (needs experiments):
- Is the skew correlation stronger with network partition vs. host-local disk slowness? (We need targeted tests that simulate network delays vs. disk IO delays.)
- Does the microbatcher produce pathological patterns that increase memory (e.g., very wide KV prefetch sets) during rebuilds?

Notes to next on-call:
- If you see kv_index_skew_ratio rising and host-level memory pressure at the same time, prioritize traffic shaping + rebuild concurrency reduction.
- Avoid immediate mass restarts of runtime pods on hot-swapping hosts; instead prefer controlled drain/migration to reduce simultaneous rebuild windows.

Appendix: quick checklist for runbook insertion (copyable):
- [ ] Open incident JIRA (template: SRE-incident-hot-swap-kv).
- [ ] Execute traffic throttle: /ops/throttle runtime-route <route> 50%
- [ ] Set dynconfig: kv.rebuild.max_concurrency=1 (and note previous value).
- [ ] Monitor kv_index_skew_ratio and microbatch_queue_length for rollback conditions.
- [ ] After stabilization: revert dynconfig and remove throttle; record timings in post-incident notes.

End of note.

-- Aisha
(on-call, eng-sre)
